title: Event-Case Correlation for Process Mining using Probabilistic Optimization
research_question: How can events lacking explicit case identifiers be assigned to process instances by combining control-flow, temporal, and data-attribute evidence?
methodology: The paper formulates event-case correlation as reconstructing a partition of an uncorrelated event log into process cases and proposes EC-SA-Data, a simulated-annealing optimization method. Its nested objectives consider conformance to a process model, support for data constraints, and variation in activity execution times. Evaluation uses four real-world BPI Challenge logs, removes or ignores their known case assignments to form the correlation task, and compares reconstructions with the ground-truth logs using trace-, n-gram-, and case-oriented similarities together with timing deviation measures. Additional experiments vary the number and correctness of domain data constraints and compare the data-aware method with an earlier variant that omits them.

key_findings.finding: Data attributes and domain constraints can materially improve reconstruction of concrete process-instance identity when explicit case identifiers are absent.

Across the reported datasets, adding data constraints improves the average trace-, n-gram-, and especially case-level similarity measures, with the paper reporting average gains of roughly 6%, 15%, and 28% respectively.
On the large BPIC17 experiment, the reported improvement in case-level similarity from using data constraints reaches approximately 46%.
Increasing the number of correct constraints generally improves reconstruction quality, while inaccurate constraints degrade the inferred correlations.
The method can operate with process models containing cyclic and parallel behavior, relaxing restrictions present in some earlier event-correlation approaches.
Computational cost grows materially on large logs; the reported BPIC17 run takes about 13 hours with ten constraints compared with about 8.6 hours without those constraints.

Despite using a metric called partial case similarity, the underlying correlation model requires every event to belong to exactly one case; the metric measures overlap between candidate and reference cases rather than a partial continuity relation.

The study does not evaluate enterprise email, chat threads, or natural-language work-item continuity, so its evidence applies to process-instance identity rather than direct communication-thread linking.

limitations: The formulation is a hard partition in which each event belongs to one and only one case, excluding overlapping or multiple-case membership.
Partial case similarity is an evaluation measure and does not provide a representation for partial, subevent, asymmetric, or non-transitive continuity.
The approach assumes that an underlying process model is available.
Useful domain data constraints must be identified, and in the experiments these are obtained through analysis of the logs rather than discovered as a fully automatic part of the method.
Runtime is substantial on the largest evaluated log and increases when more constraints are incorporated.
Correlation quality deteriorates as the number of simultaneously plausible event assignments grows in large or dense logs.
The experiments use structured process-event logs rather than enterprise email, chat, or textual work communications.
The paper does not study evolving work-item identities across longitudinal communication threads.
No public implementation is reported in the paper.
raw_claims: Process mining normally assumes that each event carries a case identifier linking it to one process instance.
When case identifiers are missing, event correlation must reconstruct which events belong together.
EC-SA-Data searches for a case assignment with simulated annealing rather than relying on a single deterministic heuristic.
The optimization incorporates process-model conformance, data constraints, and activity-time behavior.
Every event in the formal problem is assigned to one and only one reconstructed case.
The evaluation uses four BPI Challenge event logs whose original case structure provides a reference for measuring reconstruction quality.
Adding correct data constraints improves similarity between reconstructed and original logs.
Case-oriented similarity gains are larger than the average trace-level gains reported for the data-aware variant.
Incorrect constraints can steer the optimization toward worse case assignments.
The largest evaluated event log incurs multi-hour optimization runtimes.
The method supports process models with cycles and parallelism.
The paper's partial case similarity measure quantifies shared events between reconstructed and reference cases; it does not permit one event to belong partially to several cases.
The evaluated evidence concerns structured process instances rather than conversational or email-thread continuity.
